fiber-001.question: What is the basic mechanism by which an optical fiber confines light to its core?
choices: The core's refractive index is made slightly higher than the cladding's, and total internal reflection at the boundary (guiding) confines the light
The cladding's refractive index is made higher than the core's, so the cladding absorbs light leaking from the core and keeps it from escaping
A metal film on the surface of the core confines the light by mirror reflection
fiber-001.explanation: In an optical fiber, the core index n₁ is made about 0.3–1% higher than the cladding index n₂, and light striking the boundary at angles of incidence larger than the critical angle (that is, at grazing angles) is totally reflected and confined (in wave optics, it is treated as guided modes localized in the core). If the cladding index were higher than the core's, total internal reflection would not occur and light would leak into the cladding. Absorbing light in the cladding would only add loss, not confinement. Metal reflection absorbs a few percent per bounce and cannot be used for long-distance transmission involving millions of reflections. Total internal reflection is ideally lossless, which makes kilometer-scale transmission possible.

fiber-002.question: Which value is closest to the numerical aperture NA of a step-index fiber with a core index of 1.468 and a cladding index of 1.462?
fiber-002.explanation: The numerical aperture is NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = √(1.468² − 1.462²) = √(2.1550 − 2.1374) ≈ √0.0176 ≈ 0.13. The maximum acceptance angle from air is about 7.6°, from sinθ = NA. About 0.006 uses the index difference n₁ − n₂ directly, and about 0.018 is n₁² − n₂² without the square root. NA can also be written NA ≈ n₁√(2Δ) (Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ is the relative index difference); thanks to the square root, even a tiny index difference gives an NA of around 0.1. Standard single-mode fibers have an NA of about 0.1–0.14, multimode fibers about 0.2–0.3.

fiber-003.question: Light at 1550 nm is sent through a step-index fiber with a core radius of 4.1 µm and a numerical aperture of 0.12. Which correctly gives the normalized frequency (V-number, V = 2πaNA/λ) and the propagation regime?
choices: V ≈ 0.32; the light is not guided
fiber-003.explanation: V = 2πaNA/λ = 2π × 4.1×10⁻⁶ × 0.12 / 1.55×10⁻⁶ ≈ 1.99. In a step-index fiber, only the fundamental mode (LP01) propagates when V < 2.405 (the first zero of the zeroth-order Bessel function), so the fiber is single-mode. Multimode at V ≈ 2.0 gets the 2.405 threshold wrong. “Not guided” is also wrong: the fundamental mode has no cutoff and is guided however small V is (although if V is too small, the mode spreads far into the cladding and becomes sensitive to bending). About 0.32 forgets to multiply by 2π.

fiber-004.question: Which value is closest to the cutoff wavelength (above which the fiber is single-mode) of a step-index fiber with a core radius of 4.1 µm and a numerical aperture of 0.12? (Single-mode condition V < 2.405.)
fiber-004.explanation: The cutoff wavelength is where V = 2.405: λc = 2πaNA / 2.405 = 2π × 4.1 × 0.12 / 2.405 ≈ 1.29 µm. At the longer 1.31 µm and 1.55 µm bands the fiber is single-mode, while at shorter wavelengths such as 850 nm higher-order modes (such as LP11) also propagate. About 1.55 µm takes V ≈ 2.0 at the operating wavelength as the threshold, giving λ = 2πaNA/2.0; about 7.4 µm multiplies by 2.405 instead of dividing. In real fibers, higher-order modes are easily attenuated by bends, so the cutoff wavelength in a cable is shorter than the theoretical value, and standards specify the cable cutoff wavelength.

fiber-005.question: Light is transmitted 80 km through a single-mode fiber with a loss of 0.2 dB/km. If the input is 0 dBm (1 mW), which value is closest to the output power? (Ignore splice losses.)
fiber-005.explanation: The total loss is 0.2 × 80 = 16 dB, so the output is 0 − 16 = −16 dBm. Converting to mW gives 10^(−16/10) ≈ 0.025 mW, or about 25 µW. About 63 µW treats 16 dB as a factor of 1/16, mistaking decibels for the ratio itself. About 2.5 µW corresponds to −26 dBm, an order-of-magnitude error. Since 10 times is 10 dB and 2 times is about 3 dB, 16 dB can be worked out mentally as 10 dB (1/10) plus 6 dB (about 1/4), or about 1/40. In optical link design (the link budget), such losses are subtracted from the difference between transmit power and receiver sensitivity to check the margin.

fiber-006.question: What is the main reason silica fiber loss increases at shorter wavelengths, such as visible light?
choices: Rayleigh scattering from density fluctuations in the glass, whose strength is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength
Infrared absorption by lattice (molecular) vibrations of silica, whose tail extends into the visible and is stronger at shorter wavelengths
Absorption by OH groups (water) left in the glass during fabrication, whose absorption bands lie only in the visible region rather than the infrared
fiber-006.explanation: Silica glass contains tiny density fluctuations frozen in as it solidified from the melt, and they scatter light. This is Rayleigh scattering, whose strength scales as λ⁻⁴, so halving the wavelength raises the scattering loss about 16 times. The loss reaches its minimum (about 0.2 dB/km or below) in the 1.55 µm band because that is the valley between Rayleigh scattering on the short-wavelength side and infrared absorption, which rises steeply on the long-wavelength side (beyond about 1.6 µm). Infrared absorption is stronger at longer wavelengths, so it is not the cause of loss at short wavelengths. OH absorption lies in the near infrared, for example around 1.38 µm, and is not confined to visible light.

fiber-007.question: An optical pulse with a spectral width of 0.1 nm travels 50 km through a single-mode fiber with chromatic dispersion D = 17 ps/(nm·km). Which value is closest to the pulse broadening (the spread in group delay)?
fiber-007.explanation: Pulse broadening from chromatic dispersion is Δτ = D × L × Δλ = 17 × 50 × 0.1 = 85 ps. About 8.5 ps and about 850 ps get the order of magnitude of the distance or spectral width wrong. Chromatic dispersion arises because group velocity depends on wavelength (frequency), so the different wavelength components in a pulse arrive at different times. At 10 Gb/s the bit period is 100 ps, so 85 ps of broadening causes overlap with neighboring bits (intersymbol interference). Countermeasures include dispersion-compensating fiber, narrow-linewidth lasers with external modulators, and digital signal processing at the receiver.

fiber-008.question: Why is the zero-dispersion wavelength of standard single-mode fiber near 1.31 µm?
choices: Because silica absorption is lowest at 1.31 µm, so light travels without delay
Because the material dispersion of silica and the waveguide dispersion of the guiding structure cancel near 1.31 µm
Because at 1.31 µm the fiber is no longer single-mode, and the modal dispersion of higher-order modes cancels the chromatic dispersion
fiber-008.explanation: The chromatic dispersion of single-mode fiber is the sum of material dispersion, from the wavelength dependence of silica's refractive index, and waveguide dispersion, from the way the spread of light into core and cladding changes with wavelength. Silica's material dispersion is zero at about 1.27 µm and the waveguide dispersion is slightly negative, so the total is zero near 1.31 µm. Engineering the core index profile to enlarge the waveguide dispersion gives dispersion-shifted fiber with zero dispersion moved to 1.55 µm, but because four-wave mixing occurs easily in wavelength-division multiplexing, non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber that leaves a little dispersion is used instead. Dispersion is a separate phenomenon from absorption, and the single-mode condition is still satisfied at 1.31 µm.

fiber-009.question: Which correctly describes the mode field diameter (MFD) of standard single-mode fiber?
choices: It is larger than the core diameter and grows at longer wavelengths
It always equals the core diameter, regardless of wavelength
It is smaller than the core diameter and shrinks at longer wavelengths
fiber-009.explanation: The fundamental mode of a single-mode fiber is not fully confined to the core and extends into the cladding. The diameter at which the intensity falls to 1/e² of its center value is the mode field diameter; in standard fiber with a core of about 8 µm diameter, it is about 9.2 µm at 1.31 µm and about 10.4 µm at 1.55 µm, larger than the core. At longer wavelengths the V-number is smaller, confinement weakens and light spreads into the cladding, so the MFD grows. Splicing fibers with different MFDs causes coupling loss from mismatched mode shapes, and fibers with a large MFD resist nonlinear effects but are more sensitive to bending loss.

fiber-010.question: Two single-mode fibers with a mode field radius of 5.2 µm are fusion-spliced with a lateral offset of 1 µm between their axes. Which value is closest to the coupling loss caused by this offset? (Assume Gaussian modes, with transmittance T = exp(−(d/w)²).)
fiber-010.explanation: The coupling efficiency of Gaussian modes with a lateral offset is T = exp(−(d/w)²) = exp(−(1/5.2)²) ≈ exp(−0.037) ≈ 0.964. The loss is −10 log₁₀(0.964) ≈ 0.16 dB. About 0.04 dB takes (d/w)² as the loss in dB, and about 1.6 dB is an order-of-magnitude error. Because even a 1 µm offset costs 0.16 dB, fusion splicers align the cores by imaging them and keep typical splice loss at 0.05 dB or less. Differences in mode field diameter, angular misalignment and gaps between the end faces also cause loss, and their effects are combined by multiplication (addition in dB).

fiber-011.question: Light is transmitted 100 km through a fiber with a polarization mode dispersion (PMD) coefficient of 0.1 ps/√km. Which value is closest to the mean differential group delay (DGD)?
fiber-011.explanation: PMD is the difference in group velocity between the two polarization modes caused by slight birefringence in the fiber. In long fibers the orientation of the birefringence axes changes randomly, so the delay difference does not grow in proportion to distance but, like a random walk, in proportion to its square root. The mean DGD is therefore 0.1 × √100 = 1 ps. About 10 ps scales with distance as 0.1 × 100, which the coefficient's unit, ps/√km, rules out. About 0.1 ps ignores the distance. Because PMD is a statistical quantity that changes over time with temperature and vibration, high-speed systems at 40 Gb/s and above compensate it adaptively with digital signal processing at the receiver.

fiber-012.question: Which pump wavelengths are commonly used for erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs)?
fiber-012.explanation: An EDFA sends pump light into fiber doped with erbium ions (Er³⁺) to create a population inversion, and amplifies signals around 1530–1565 nm (the C band) by stimulated emission. Pumping uses semiconductor lasers at 980 nm (three-level-like pumping with low noise) or 1480 nm (pumping the top of the same band as the signal directly, with high conversion efficiency), matching erbium's absorption bands. Erbium does not absorb at 1310 nm, so it cannot be used for pumping. Light at the signal wavelength of 1550 nm cannot lift ions into the level that amplifies the signal. EDFAs made it possible to amplify many wavelengths at once without converting light back to electricity, enabling high-capacity long-haul transmission with wavelength-division multiplexing.

fiber-013.question: Roughly what is the theoretical lower limit (quantum limit) of the noise figure (NF) of an EDFA with sufficiently high gain?
fiber-013.explanation: In an optical amplifier, spontaneous emission is amplified along with the signal and becomes noise (ASE). With complete inversion and high gain, the noise figure — the ratio of input to output signal-to-noise ratios — has a quantum-mechanical lower limit of 2, or about 3 dB. 0 dB is the ideal of adding no noise, which a conventional phase-insensitive amplifier cannot reach (a phase-sensitive amplifier can in principle). About 10 dB is not the limit but a degraded value seen with incomplete inversion or large loss at the input. Practical EDFAs have an NF of about 4–6 dB, and a low NF is generally considered easier to achieve with 980 nm pumping than with 1480 nm pumping.

fiber-014.question: A narrow-linewidth continuous-wave laser is launched at high power into a long single-mode fiber. Above a certain power, light returning toward the input suddenly increases and the output saturates. Which nonlinear effect is the likely main cause?
fiber-014.explanation: Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) is an interaction between light and acoustic phonons (sound waves) in which light is scattered backward at a frequency about 11 GHz lower (for silica in the 1.55 µm band). Because the Brillouin gain bandwidth is narrow, a few tens of MHz, narrower-linewidth light drives it more efficiently, and its threshold of a few milliwatts is the lowest among nonlinear effects. Above threshold, much of the input light is reflected and the transmittable power saturates. Self-phase modulation changes a beam's own phase according to its power and sends no light backward. Four-wave mixing creates new wavelengths among several existing ones and is not a main problem for single-wavelength continuous light. SBS can be suppressed by frequency-modulating the laser to broaden its linewidth.

fiber-015.question: Which value is closest to the effective length (the length over which nonlinear effects effectively act, Leff = (1 − e^(−αL))/α, with α the attenuation coefficient in 1/km) of 100 km of fiber with a loss of 0.2 dB/km?
fiber-015.explanation: First convert the loss in dB/km to an attenuation coefficient: α = 0.2 / (10 log₁₀e) = 0.2 / 4.343 ≈ 0.046 /km. Since αL ≈ 4.6, e^(−4.6) ≈ 0.01, and Leff = (1 − 0.01)/0.046 ≈ 21.5 km, or about 22 km. However long the fiber, the power decays exponentially, so nonlinear effects act only over roughly the first 20 km from the input. About 100 km ignores the loss, and about 5 km is the unit error of using 0.2 dB/km directly as α and computing 1/0.2. Because the nonlinear phase is set by γPLeff, lengthening the span between repeaters does not increase nonlinear effects very much.

fiber-016.question: Why is the core index of a graded-index multimode fiber made highest at the center and lowered roughly parabolically toward the outside?
choices: Only light near the center of the core satisfies the condition for total internal reflection, so higher-order modes are removed and the fiber operates single-mode
Grading the index removes density fluctuations in the glass, eliminating Rayleigh scattering and making the loss an order of magnitude lower than a step-index fiber
Rays that swing far out travel a longer path but through faster, lower-index regions, so the differences in arrival time between modes become small
fiber-016.explanation: In a step-index multimode fiber, a ray traveling along the axis and a ray zigzagging at a large angle have different path lengths through the same index, so they arrive at different times (modal dispersion). With a parabolic index profile, rays that swing far out take a longer path but pass through the faster, lower-index regions, so the delay is canceled and modal dispersion is greatly reduced (by more than two orders of magnitude for an ideal profile). Many modes still propagate, so the fiber does not become single-mode. The loss is set mainly by the glass and its impurities, and the index profile does not eliminate Rayleigh scattering.

fiber-017.question: For a step-index multimode fiber with a core index of 1.48 and a cladding index of 1.46, which value is closest to the maximum difference in arrival time caused by different ray paths over 1 km? Use Δτ ≈ L(n₁ − n₂)/c with c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s.
fiber-017.explanation: The delay difference between a ray along the axis and a ray at just the critical angle is approximately Δτ ≈ L(n₁ − n₂)/c = 1000 × 0.02 / (3.0×10⁸) ≈ 6.7×10⁻⁸ s, or about 67 ns. About 6.7 ns is off by a factor of ten, and about 4.9 µs is the transit time over 1 km itself (Ln₁/c), not a difference in arrival time. With pulses spreading by about 67 ns, the bit interval must be long enough to keep neighboring pulses apart, limiting the bit rate–distance product to about 10 Mbit/s·km. Graded-index fibers and single-mode fibers, which carry only one mode, reduce this spreading.

fiber-018.question: Which correctly describes the loss that arises when a standard single-mode fiber is bent tightly (macrobend loss)?
choices: Longer wavelengths spread the mode further into the cladding and are more bend-sensitive, so the loss rises more readily at 1550 nm or 1625 nm than at 1310 nm
Shorter wavelengths spread the mode further into the cladding and are more bend-sensitive, so the loss rises more readily at 1310 nm than at 1550 nm
It is scattering from tiny cracks in the glass caused by bending, so it rises equally at all wavelengths and remains after the bend is released
fiber-018.explanation: In a bend, the outer tail of the mode would have to travel faster to keep the wavefront together, and light beyond a certain radius radiates into the cladding and is lost. A longer wavelength lowers the V number and enlarges the mode field diameter, so the tail extending into the cladding widens and bend loss rises sharply with wavelength. Measuring at 1550 nm or 1625 nm is therefore effective for checking bends in cabling. Saying shorter wavelengths are more sensitive gets the trend backward. Bend loss is radiation caused by the breakdown of guiding, and unless cracks form it disappears when the bend is released. Bend-insensitive fibers confine light with a low-index trench in the cladding.

fiber-019.question: Some fiber connectors have their end faces polished at about 8° to the axis rather than perpendicular (APC connectors). What is their main purpose?
choices: Light meets the end face at Brewster's angle, so the reflection becomes zero and the insertion loss vanishes for every polarization
The angled face increases the contact area and makes the joint mechanically stronger, but the amount of back-reflected light is the same as for a flat face
Light reflected at the end face escapes into the cladding instead of returning in the core, greatly reducing reflections back to lasers or receivers
fiber-019.explanation: If a gap opens between perpendicular end faces, about 4% (about −14 dB) of the light is reflected at the glass–air boundary and travels straight back down the core. With the face angled at about 8°, the reflected light travels about 16° off the axis, well beyond the few degrees the core can guide, so it is lost in the cladding instead of returning. This keeps back-reflection to about −60 dB or lower, and APC connectors are used with narrow-linewidth lasers sensitive to feedback and in analog video transmission. 8° is far smaller than Brewster's angle for glass (about 56°), so the design does not rely on polarization-dependent transmission, nor is it a measure for mechanical strength.

fiber-020.question: A standard single-mode fiber with a mode field radius of 5.2 µm is butt-coupled with no axial offset to a fiber with a mode field radius of 4.0 µm. Which value is closest to the coupling loss caused by the mismatch in mode field size? Assume Gaussian modes, with transmittance T = [2w₁w₂/(w₁² + w₂²)]².
choices: 0 dB (there is no loss if the axes are aligned)
fiber-020.explanation: T = [2 × 5.2 × 4.0 / (5.2² + 4.0²)]² = (41.6/43.04)² ≈ 0.934, so the loss is −10 log₁₀(0.934) ≈ 0.30 dB. The formula comes from the overlap integral of two Gaussian fields and depends only on the ratio of the radii, so the loss is the same in either direction. About 1.1 dB takes the radius ratio 4.0/5.2 itself as the transmittance, underestimating the overlap. Even with the axes aligned, fields of different widths do not overlap completely, so the loss is not 0 dB. When joining fibers or waveguides with very different mode field sizes, tapers that change the size gradually are used to reduce this loss.

fiber-021.question: Light at a wavelength of 850 nm travels through a step-index multimode fiber with a core radius of 25 µm and a numerical aperture of 0.20. Which value is closest to the approximate number of guided modes (M ≈ V²/2, V = 2πaNA/λ)?
fiber-021.explanation: V = 2π × 25 × 0.20 / 0.85 ≈ 37.0, so the number of modes is M ≈ V²/2 ≈ 36.96² / 2 ≈ 683, about 680 (counting the two polarization states separately). About 37 wrongly takes the V number itself as the number of modes, and about 1400 forgets to divide V² by 2. The number of modes grows as the square of V, so a larger core or a higher numerical aperture makes it easier to launch light but increases the number of modes and the modal dispersion. Compared with the single-mode condition V < 2.405, where only one mode remains, this shows that hundreds of modes propagate simultaneously in a multimode fiber.

fiber-022.question: A silica fiber with a refractive index of 1.45 is cleaved so that its end face is perpendicular to the axis and is left in air. Which value is closest to the return loss (−10 log₁₀ R) due to Fresnel reflection at the end face? (Assume normal incidence.)
fiber-022.explanation: The reflectance at normal incidence is R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))² = (0.45/2.45)² ≈ 0.034, about 3.4%, so the return loss is −10 log₁₀ 0.034 ≈ 14.7 dB, about 15 dB. About 29 dB applies 20 log to a power ratio, and about 7 dB converts the amplitude reflection coefficient of 0.18 to dB with 10 log. A reflection of about 15 dB is a large back-reflection for narrow-linewidth lasers and high-speed optical links, causing noise and unstable operation. The return loss is raised to several tens of dB by filling the gap between end faces with index-matching material, by PC polishing so that the end faces touch, or by an angle-polished APC connector that sends the reflected light into the cladding.

fiber-023.question: In the loss spectrum of a silica optical fiber, a loss peak sometimes appears near a wavelength of 1383 nm. Which correctly gives the cause of this peak and how to reduce it?
choices: It is a Rayleigh-scattering peak caused by density fluctuations in the glass, and it can be reduced by drawing the fiber thinner
It is an infrared-absorption peak of silica itself (Si-O bond vibrations), and it can be reduced by adding more germanium
It is an overtone absorption of hydroxyl (OH) vibrations in the glass, and it can be reduced with a low-OH fiber dehydrated during manufacture
fiber-023.explanation: The loss peak near 1383 nm is the overtone absorption of the stretching vibration of OH groups in the glass (whose fundamental absorption is at about 2.7 µm). Even a trace of OH causes a large loss, so in low-water-peak (low-OH) fibers, which are dehydrated during manufacture, this peak almost disappears and the wide band from 1260 to 1625 nm can be used for communication. Rayleigh scattering simply decreases smoothly as the inverse fourth power of wavelength and does not create a peak at a particular wavelength. Infrared absorption by Si-O bond vibrations forms the tail of loss that rises steeply at wavelengths longer than 1.6 µm, not an isolated peak at 1383 nm. Germanium is added to raise the core index; it does not reduce OH absorption.

fiber-024.question: Dispersion-shifted fiber (DSF), whose zero-dispersion wavelength was moved to 1.55 µm, was advantageous for single-wavelength transmission but proved unsuitable for wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) in the 1.55 µm band. Which correctly gives the main reason and the fiber that came into use afterward?
choices: With nearly zero dispersion the channels stay phase-matched and four-wave mixing becomes strong, so non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber, which retains a little dispersion, is used
With nearly zero dispersion the threshold for stimulated Brillouin scattering drops sharply, so a special fiber with a thinner core and a smaller effective area is used for WDM instead
With nearly zero dispersion the EDFA gain does not become flat across wavelength, so only standard single-mode fiber with its zero dispersion at 1.31 µm is used for WDM
fiber-024.explanation: Four-wave mixing is efficient when the phases of the channel signals stay aligned. With nearly zero dispersion, channels at different wavelengths travel at the same speed and phase matching is maintained over long distances, so the newly generated frequencies fall on other channels and cause noise and crosstalk. Non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber (NZ-DSF), which deliberately keeps a dispersion of a few ps/(nm·km) in the 1.55 µm band, therefore came into use. The threshold for stimulated Brillouin scattering is set by the linewidth and effective area, not by dispersion, and a smaller effective area actually makes nonlinear effects stronger. The flatness of the EDFA gain has nothing to do with the dispersion of the fiber.

fiber-025.question: Which correctly describes fiber Raman amplification, in which a strong pump is launched into the transmission fiber itself to amplify the signal?
choices: Because it uses erbium energy levels, gain is available only around 1530–1565 nm, and changing the pump wavelength does not change the gain band
Because the gain is maximum at the pump wavelength itself, a strong beam at the same wavelength as the signal must be launched as the pump
A gain peak appears about 13 THz (about 100 nm in the 1.55 µm band) below the pump frequency, so the gain band is chosen by the pump wavelength
fiber-025.explanation: In fiber Raman amplification, stimulated Raman scattering by molecular vibrations of silica transfers energy from the pump to a signal at lower frequency (longer wavelength). The gain peak lies about 13 THz below the pump frequency, so, for example, a pump near 1450 nm amplifies signals near 1550 nm. Because the gain band is set by the pump wavelength, combining several pumps at different wavelengths creates a wide, flat gain. It is distributed amplification, with gain spread gradually along the whole transmission fiber, so the signal never becomes too weak, which is also advantageous for noise. A gain band determined by erbium energy levels is the property of an EDFA. No gain appears at the pump wavelength itself either.

fiber-026.question: Light with a power of 100 mW is launched into a single-mode fiber with an effective area A_eff = 80 µm². Which value is closest to the intensity in the core (power ÷ effective area)?
fiber-026.explanation: 80 µm² = 80×10⁻¹² m² = 8.0×10⁻⁷ cm², so the intensity is 0.1 W / 8.0×10⁻⁷ cm² ≈ 1.25×10⁵ W/cm² (1.25×10⁹ W/m²). Even at only 100 mW, the tiny area makes the intensity a million times that of sunlight at the ground (about 0.1 W/cm²). In a fiber this intensity is maintained over tens of km, so even in silica, with its small nonlinear index, self-phase modulation and four-wave mixing cannot be ignored. About 1.3×10⁹ W/cm² mistakes the value in W/m² for W/cm², and about 1.3×10³ W/cm² gets the power of ten wrong when converting µm² to cm². Fibers with a large effective area are used to lower the intensity and suppress nonlinear effects.

fiber-027.question: A polarization-maintaining fiber has a difference in effective index between its two polarization axes (modal birefringence) of B = 5.0×10⁻⁴. Which value is closest to the beat length at 1.55 µm, L_B = λ/B, the length over which the phase difference between the two polarizations reaches 2π?
fiber-027.explanation: L_B = λ/B = 1.55×10⁻⁶ m / 5.0×10⁻⁴ = 3.1×10⁻³ m, about 3.1 mm. A shorter beat length means larger birefringence and a larger difference in propagation constant between the two polarizations, so bends and stresses hardly couple them and linear polarization launched along an axis is preserved. Ordinary single-mode fiber has a birefringence of about 10⁻⁷ and a beat length of about 10 m, and its polarization wanders as the light travels. About 3.1 m gets the power of ten wrong in converting µm and mm. About 0.78 mm is the length for a π/2 phase difference (the equivalent of a quarter-wave plate), not the 2π that defines the beat length.

fiber-028.question: High-power fiber lasers and fiber amplifiers often use double-clad fiber, with the pump light launched into the inner cladding. Which explains why?
choices: Keeping the pump outside the doped core means the pump is not absorbed in the core and only the signal is amplified, reducing noise
A wide, high-NA inner cladding accepts high-power pump light of poor beam quality, which is absorbed as it crosses the core
The inner cladding has a higher index than the core, so the signal also spreads into the cladding, enlarging its area and suppressing nonlinear effects
fiber-028.explanation: High-power diode lasers contain many modes and have poor beam quality, so they cannot be coupled efficiently into a single-mode core about 10 µm across. In a double-clad fiber, the core is surrounded by an inner cladding hundreds of µm across with a large numerical aperture, itself enclosed by a lower-index layer that guides the pump. Pump light traveling in the inner cladding is absorbed by the dopant ions each time it crosses the core. In this way pump light of poor beam quality is converted into high-quality single-mode laser light. The pump is absorbed in the core, so the idea of keeping it out of the core is backward. The inner cladding has a lower index than the core, and the signal remains confined to the core.

fiber-029.question: Two single-mode fibers are laid side by side, heated, stretched and fused to make a fused biconical taper coupler. Which correctly describes how it works?
choices: In the fused region the two cores merge into one thick core and light is divided equally between the outputs by geometric optics, so the split ratio does not depend on wavelength
In the thinned region the mode spreads into the cladding and couples to the neighboring fiber; the coupling length and wavelength set the split ratio, so it can also combine 980 nm and 1550 nm
Light is partly reflected at the fused interface and passes into the other fiber, so the split ratio is set by the interface reflectance and not by the length of the stretched region
fiber-029.explanation: In the stretched, thinned region the cores shrink and the mode spreads out of the core into the cladding, overlapping the mode of the neighboring fiber. Light then passes back and forth between the two periodically (the same principle as a directional coupler), and the split ratio at the outputs is set by the length of the coupling region and the coupling strength. Because the coupling strength depends on wavelength, a suitable length sends one wavelength to one output and another to the other, so these couplers are also used as WDM couplers that combine EDFA pump light (980 nm) with the signal (1550 nm). It does not divide light by geometric optics, so the ratio does vary with wavelength, and it does not rely on reflection at a fused interface.

fiber-030.question: Compared with silica single-mode fiber, which correctly describes plastic optical fiber (POF) with a PMMA (acrylic) core?
choices: Its loss in the visible is about 0.2 dB/km, lower than silica, but its thin core makes splicing and connection difficult, so it is used only for long-haul trunk lines
Its loss is lowest at 1550 nm, so the same lasers and amplifiers as for silica can be used directly, making it suited to long-distance links
Its core is thick, about 1 mm, with a large NA, so it is easy to connect, but its loss is about 150 dB/km even at 650 nm, so it is used over short distances
fiber-030.explanation: PMMA POF has a thick core about 1 mm across and a large numerical aperture of about 0.5, so end preparation and alignment are easy and it tolerates bending well. On the other hand, overtones of C–H bond vibrations cause absorption, so the low-loss windows are confined to the visible (around 520, 570 and 650 nm), and even there the loss is about 70–200 dB/km (around 150 dB/km near the commonly used 650 nm), orders of magnitude above the roughly 0.2 dB/km of silica. At 1550 nm in the infrared the absorption is very large, so lasers and EDFAs designed for silica cannot be used. POF is therefore used for short links of up to a few tens of meters, such as in homes, offices, cars and inside equipment. Saying its visible loss is lower than silica's confuses it with the value for silica.

fiber-031.question: Two points 1000 km apart are linked by a single-mode fiber with a group index of 1.468. Which value is closest to the one-way transit time of an optical signal? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
fiber-031.explanation: Signal energy travels at the group velocity v_g = c/n_g, so the delay is τ = n_g L / c = 1.468 × 1.0×10⁶ m / 3.0×10⁸ m/s ≈ 4.9×10⁻³ s, about 4.9 ms. That is about 4.9 µs per km, and remembering "about 5 µs per km of fiber" is handy for estimates. About 3.3 ms uses the speed of light in vacuum; in the fiber the signal travels about 1.47 times slower. About 9.8 ms is the round-trip time, which is not what a one-way delay asks for (it is the value measured in round-trip techniques such as OTDR). Over long links this propagation delay sets a lower limit on response time that faster signal processing cannot reduce.

fiber-032.question: A single-mode fiber has a chromatic dispersion of D = 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm. Which value is closest to its group-velocity dispersion β₂? (β₂ = −Dλ²/(2πc), c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
fiber-032.explanation: In consistent units, D = 17 ps/(nm·km) = 17×10⁻⁶ s/m². Then β₂ = −17×10⁻⁶ × (1.55×10⁻⁶)² / (2π × 3.0×10⁸) ≈ −2.17×10⁻²⁶ s²/m, and since 1 ps²/km = 10⁻²⁷ s²/m this is about −21.7 ps²/km, i.e. about −22 ps²/km. The 1.55 µm band, where D is positive, is a region of anomalous dispersion with negative β₂, in which higher-frequency (shorter-wavelength) components travel faster. About +22 ps²/km drops the minus sign; D and β₂ have opposite signs. About −0.022 ps²/km mishandles a factor of 10³ in converting nm and km.

fiber-033.question: In a hollow-core fiber, the core is air and is surrounded by thin glass membranes or a fine periodic structure, so most of the light travels in air. Which statement correctly compares it with a conventional silica single-mode fiber?
choices: Light is confined by interference of reflections from the surrounding structure, and with a group index near 1 the delay is about 30% shorter and nonlinear effects are smaller
Air has a higher index than glass, so light is confined by total internal reflection as usual, and the group index equals that of silica, so the delay is unchanged
Rayleigh scattering is stronger in air than in glass, raising the loss, and air molecules strengthen nonlinear effects, so it is unsuitable for high power
fiber-033.explanation: The refractive index of air is lower than that of the surrounding glass, so total internal reflection cannot confine light in an air core. Hollow-core fibers confine light by interference of reflections, through antiresonance in thin glass membranes around the core or through a photonic bandgap in a periodic structure. Because most of the light travels in air, the group index is close to 1, and the delay is about 3.3 µs per km, roughly 30% shorter than in silica fiber (group index about 1.47). The small overlap with glass also greatly reduces nonlinear effects and material absorption. The premise that air has a higher index than glass is backwards. Air molecules are far less dense than glass, so both Rayleigh scattering and nonlinear effects are smaller.

fiber-034.question: Linearly polarized light from a narrow-linewidth laser is launched into an ordinary (non-polarization-maintaining) single-mode fiber, and the polarization of the output is examined after a few metres or more. Which describes the output polarization correctly?
choices: The core is circularly symmetric with no birefringence, so the input linear polarization is preserved and can be fully extinguished with a polarizer
The polarization is always scrambled in the fiber, so the output is unpolarized and its brightness does not change as a polarizer is rotated
Small birefringence that varies randomly along the fiber generally makes the output elliptical, and the state changes with bending and temperature
fiber-034.explanation: A real fiber has small birefringence whose orientation and magnitude vary along its length, caused by slight core distortions, bends, twists and external stress. The output is therefore generally elliptically polarized, and the state drifts as the bends or the temperature change. Preservation of polarization by a circularly symmetric core applies only to an ideal fiber; because real fibers do not preserve it, polarization-maintaining fibers are made. With narrow-linewidth light the two polarization components stay mutually coherent, so the light is not depolarized: the output remains fully polarized and its brightness changes as a polarizer is rotated. Hence polarization controllers or polarization-maintaining fiber are used in front of polarization-sensitive components.

fiber-035.question: When an erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) amplifies a fast intensity-modulated signal such as 10 Gbit/s, the gain hardly depends on the bit sequence (there is almost no pattern effect). What is the main reason?
choices: The gain bandwidth is tens of nm wide, so the whole modulation-broadened spectrum receives the same gain and the waveform is not distorted
The Er³⁺ upper-level lifetime is about 10 ms, so the gain cannot follow bit-by-bit changes and is set only by the average power
Fiber nonlinearity cancels the gain changes, so gain saturation recovers faster than the bit period
fiber-035.explanation: Gain saturation results from changes in the population inversion, whose speed is set by the upper-level lifetime. The Er³⁺ upper level lives about 10 ms, far longer than a bit (100 ps at 10 Gbit/s), so the inversion responds only to the average signal power and the gain hardly varies with the bit sequence. A semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA), with a carrier lifetime of a nanosecond or less, does show pattern effects and crosstalk between wavelength channels. A wide gain bandwidth is a spectral property and is separate from the speed of the time response. Nonlinear effects do not cancel gain saturation either. Even in an EDFA, however, a sudden change in the number of channels causes gain transients on a millisecond time scale.

fiber-036.question: Which value is closest to the mode field diameter (MFD) of a step-index single-mode fibre with a core radius of 4.1 µm and a V number of 2.0? (Use Marcuse's formula w/a ≈ 0.65 + 1.619V^(−1.5) + 2.879V^(−6), where w is the mode field radius and a the core radius.)
fiber-036.explanation: w/a ≈ 0.65 + 1.619 × 2.0^(−1.5) + 2.879 × 2.0^(−6) = 0.65 + 0.572 + 0.045 ≈ 1.27, so w ≈ 1.27 × 4.1 ≈ 5.2 µm and MFD = 2w ≈ 10.4 µm. About 5.2 µm is the mode field radius, which must be doubled to give the diameter. About 8.2 µm is the core diameter; the field extends into the cladding, so the MFD is larger than the core. The smaller the V number (the longer the wavelength), the larger the V^(−1.5) term and the wider the MFD. This mode field radius is the quantity used to estimate splice losses.

fiber-037.question: An LED whose emitting area is much smaller than the fibre core (with a Lambertian pattern, intensity proportional to cosθ, where θ is the angle from the normal) is butted against the end of a step-index multimode fibre with a numerical aperture of 0.20. Which value is closest to the fraction of the light emitted into the forward hemisphere that enters the fibre? (Ignore end-face reflection.)
fiber-037.explanation: For a Lambertian emitter, integrating the cosθ weighting over solid angle shows that the fraction of the forward-hemisphere flux inside a cone of half-angle θ is sin²θ. The sine of the acceptance angle is the numerical aperture, so the fraction is NA² = 0.20² = 0.04, or about 4%. About 2% assumes that the light is emitted equally in all directions and uses the solid-angle ratio 1 − cosθ (θ ≈ 11.5°), ignoring that a Lambertian source is brightest near the normal. About 20% takes the numerical aperture itself as the fraction. If the emitting area is larger than the core, the area ratio multiplies this as well and the coupling efficiency falls further.

fiber-038.question: A solid-core photonic crystal fibre, whose cladding consists of a periodic array of small air holes around a silica core, can remain single-mode down to short wavelengths when the hole size is chosen properly (endlessly single-mode operation). Why?
choices: Most of the light travels in the air holes, so even at shorter wavelengths it is unaffected by the silica and V stays constant whatever the wavelength
At shorter wavelengths the light keeps to the silica between the holes, raising the cladding's effective index, so the index contrast falls and V stays nearly constant
Light in higher-order modes is readily absorbed at the inner walls of the air holes, so only the fundamental mode survives even as V rises at shorter wavelengths
fiber-038.explanation: In an ordinary step-index fibre the index contrast is nearly fixed, so V = 2πaNA/λ grows inversely with wavelength and the fibre becomes multimode at short wavelengths. In a cladding of air holes, shorter-wavelength light keeps out of the holes and gathers in the silica, so the cladding's effective index approaches that of silica and the effective numerical aperture decreases with wavelength. The two effects cancel, V stays below the cutoff value, and the fibre is single-mode over a wide wavelength range. Light guided in air is the case of hollow-core fibres; in a solid-core fibre the light travels in the silica core. Neither air nor silica absorbs light in higher-order modes.

fiber-039.question: The loss of a silica single-mode fibre is lowest near a wavelength of 1.55 µm, about 0.2 dB/km. Why is the loss lowest at this wavelength?
choices: Rayleigh scattering (∝ λ⁻⁴) rises toward shorter wavelengths and Si–O vibrational absorption toward longer ones, leaving a valley near 1.55 µm
1.55 µm is the emission wavelength of erbium, and the gain of erbium doped into the fibre effectively cancels the loss at this wavelength
Near 1.55 µm the chromatic dispersion of silica is zero, so pulses travel without spreading and the scattering loss is also lowest there
fiber-039.explanation: The loss of silica glass is mainly the sum of two contributions. Rayleigh scattering from density fluctuations falls as λ⁻⁴ toward longer wavelengths, whereas the absorption tail from Si–O bond vibrations rises steeply beyond about 1.6 µm. Where the two curves cross there is a valley near 1.55 µm, giving the minimum of about 0.2 dB/km. EDFAs are used in this band because the amplifier was chosen to match the low-loss window; transmission fibre is not doped with erbium. The zero-dispersion wavelength of standard single-mode fibre is near 1.31 µm, and dispersion is a property separate from scattering loss.

fiber-040.question: To extract light reflected by a fibre Bragg grating (FBG), a three-port optical circulator is often used instead of a 50:50 fibre coupler. Which combination correctly describes what the circulator does and its advantage?
choices: It diffracts the light from port 1 to a port that depends on wavelength, so only the FBG's reflection wavelength is taken out at port 3
It routes light non-reciprocally from port 1 to port 2 and from port 2 to port 3, avoiding a coupler's roughly 6 dB round-trip loss
It splits the input by polarization between ports 2 and 3, so the round-trip loss is 3 dB lower than with a coupler
fiber-040.explanation: An optical circulator combines non-reciprocal polarization rotation in a Faraday rotator with polarization-splitting elements to send light from each port to the next one in turn. With the FBG on port 2, the transmitted light reaches the FBG with little loss, and the reflected light exits at port 3 instead of returning to the source. A 50:50 coupler loses 3 dB on the way out and another 3 dB on the way back, about 6 dB in total, and sends half of the reflected light back toward the source. Sorting light by wavelength is the job of a demultiplexer such as an AWG; the circulator itself is not wavelength-selective. A device that divided the light by polarization would lose half of the light meant for port 2.
